> 將為胠篋、探囊、發匱之盜而為守備，則必攝緘縢、固扃鐍；此世俗之所謂知也。

To guard against the thief who will pry the box, probe the bag, break the chest, you tie the cords tight and bolt the locks. This is what the world calls wisdom.

Then the great thief arrives, carries the whole chest off on his back, and is only worried that you did not tie it well enough.

## 胠: prying from the side

胠 is flesh with 去 as phonetic; its original sense is the flank, the side of the ribs. Extended: to pry open from the side.

箧 is a small box. 胠篋: not smashing the box — finding the seam and entering from the side.

The method of the chapter is the same as the method it describes. It does not attack 仁義 head-on. It enters from the flank.

## 緘縢, 扃鐍: the whole vocabulary of defense

緘縢: the cords you tie with. 扃: the door bar. 鐍: the lock catch.

Together they are every safeguard there is. And their exact limit is stated precisely: they stop the petty thief, not the great one — because the great thief takes the box.

## 田成子: the theft that included the statutes

田成子 killed the ruler of Qi and took the state — 并與其聖知之法而盜之, and he took the sagely statutes along with it.

He stole the territory and the ancestral temples and the local ordinances. So he carries the name of thief and enjoys the security of 堯 and 舜: small states do not dare criticize, large states do not dare attack.

This is the chapter's coldest step: 仁義禮法 is not a natural amulet. It can change owners. Whoever holds it holds the sentence "I am legitimate" — and once legitimacy can be transferred, it no longer protects the good. It protects the holder.

## 盜亦有道: five virtues, no立场

To guess what is inside the house is 聖. To enter first is 勇. To cover the retreat is 義. To judge whether it can be done is 智. To divide the loot evenly is 仁.

All five, and then you can be a great thief.

This is the blade of the chapter: 聖、勇、義、智、仁 have no side. They work as well for anyone. The virtues are not corrupt because thieves use them; they were always usable.

## 聖人不死，大盜不止

This line has been cursed for two thousand years, mostly by people who think 莊子 wants sages dead.

He is saying something else: once a thing is established as 天下之利器 — the sharp instrument of the world — someone will come to seize it. And whoever seizes it will use your rules to protect what they took.

## 符璽: trust made into an object

符 is a tally split in two; 璽 is a seal. Both are trust materialized — the sentence "what I say can be relied on," manufactured into an object that can be handed to someone else.

The moment it becomes an object, it can be taken.

## 玄同

玄: dark, undifferentiated. 同: one. Together: the oneness after division has been dissolved.

Not everything crushed into a lump. Each keeping its own clarity, each holding its own nature, and no one measuring the others against a standard. 老子 uses the same two characters in chapter 65, for the same thing.

## 竊鉤者誅，竊國者為諸侯

A man who steals a belt hook is executed; a man who steals a state becomes a lord.

The line is not a comparison of amounts. It is a statement about who is holding the ruler.

## 好知: the real charge

The final section moves the indictment off the thief and onto 好知 — the love of cleverness in high places.

When those above love knowledge, the people below stretch their necks and stand on tiptoe to chase the worthy; they leave their families and their work, and their footprints fill the roads between states.

則是好知之過也 — the fault lies with the one who set the standard.

## The test

Name one rule you rely on to be right — a policy, a norm, a principle you cite. Then run the 胠 test: if someone took this rule and used it against you, would it still hold? If the answer is that it would work perfectly for them, you are holding a 符 that can be handed over.
